objectives: Explain and locate Uses of Excel and Workbook and worksheet.
Independently create My First Excel Workbook.

lessons.introduction: Excel is spreadsheet software for organizing data, calculating results and producing reports. A workbook is a file; a worksheet is a grid inside it. Practice with fictional school records.
lessons.explanation:
Workbook: an Excel file containing one or more worksheets.

Worksheet: a tabbed grid of cells; rows are numbered and columns use letters.

Cell address: column followed by row; B2 is column B, row 2. The active cell receives input.

Formula Bar: shows or edits the active cell contents. Name Box: shows its address and can navigate to a range.

Ribbon: tabs containing commands. Sheet tabs switch worksheets. Status Bar shows selection summaries and zoom.
lessons.guided_practice:
1. Open your authorized Excel installation; choose Blank workbook. Identify Home, Formula Bar, Name Box, sheet tabs and Status Bar.
2. Click A1 and type Student Name; press Tab and enter Grade Level in B1 and Section in C1. Enter fictional values in A2:C2.
3. Click the Name Box, type B2 and press Enter. Check that column B and row 2 intersect at the active cell; use arrow keys to navigate.
4. Double-click Sheet1 and rename it Student Info. Use the plus button to add a scratch sheet, switch tabs, then return to Student Info.
5. Choose File > Save As and a school-approved folder. Select Excel Workbook (.xlsx) and enter My_First_Excel_Workbook.xlsx. Ctrl+S updates this file; Save As makes a separate copy.
6. Close the workbook, reopen it with File > Open, and verify A1:C2 and the worksheet name. Close Excel only after saving.
lessons.activity:
1. Create a blank workbook and enter the exact headings in A1:C1.
2. Enter your practice student details in A2:C2; use fictional personal information.
3. Rename Sheet1 to Student Info, save with the specified filename, close and reopen.
4. Check all six cells and explain the address of the active cell in your reflection.

objectives: Explain and locate Text and numeric entry, edit and clear cells and Copy, Cut, Paste, Undo, Redo.

lessons.introduction: Consistent headings, readable widths and appropriate number formats make school records easier to inspect. Formatting changes appearance; it does not repair incorrect data.
lessons.explanation:
Fill Handle: small square at the selection corner used to copy values/formulas or extend a series.

Wrap Text: displays long content on multiple lines inside a cell.

Number format: changes display; 0.25 formatted as Percentage displays 25%. Currency displays money, and Date formats date serial values.

Merge & Center: combines cells and retains only the upper-left value; avoid merging the body of a data table.
lessons.guided_practice:
1. Enter Subject, Teacher, Schedule and Room in A1:D1. Add English, Mathematics, Science, Filipino and TLE in A2:A6 and fictional details in B2:D6.
2. Double-click a cell or press F2 to edit. Delete clears contents; Home > Clear offers additional options. On a scratch cell practice Ctrl+C, Ctrl+V, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y.
3. Select A1:D1; use Home > Font for a readable font/size, Bold and fill color. Center headings, add borders to A1:D6, use Wrap Text for long schedules, and AutoFit column widths.
4. On a scratch area enter 1 and 2, select both and drag the Fill Handle to extend the series. Compare this with dragging one value, which can repeat it.
5. Practice Italic, Underline and font color on a temporary note. Enter 0.25, a money value and an unambiguous date in separate cells; compare Percentage, Currency and Date formats.
6. Adjust row height so wrapped text is visible. Try Merge & Center only above a scratch table with otherwise empty cells, then undo. Remove scratch content and save the subject list.

2. Bold and center headings, add readable header fill and borders.
3. Adjust column widths and row heights; use Wrap Text where needed.

lessons.title: Basic Formulas and Operators
objectives: Explain and locate Formula begins with = and Cell references.
Independently create Simple Grade Calculator.
Verify the saved workbook, correct errors and explain the result.
lessons.introduction: Formulas recalculate when referenced scores change. Cell references let you update data without rewriting every calculation.
lessons.explanation:
Formula: an expression beginning with = that calculates a result.

Relative reference: B2 changes to B3 when a formula is copied down one row.

Operator precedence: exponentiation precedes multiplication/division, which precede addition/subtraction; parentheses make the intended grouping explicit.

#DIV/0!: a formula divides by zero or an empty divisor. #VALUE!: an incompatible value is used in a calculation.
lessons.guided_practice:
1. Enter Student, Quiz, Activity, Exam, Total and Average in A1:F1. Put five fictional names and scores in A2:D6.
2. Click E2 and type =B2+C2+D2. Press Enter; inspect the formula in the Formula Bar and the total in the cell.
3. In F2 type =E2/3. Compare it with =(B2+C2+D2)/3 in a scratch cell; both average the three scores.
4. Select E2:F2 and drag the Fill Handle through row 6. Inspect E3 and F3; references must have changed to row 3.
5. Change one score and check both results recalculate. On scratch cells compare =10+5*2 (20) with =(10+5)*2 (30), =10-5 (5), =10/5 (2), =2^3 (8) and =10*5 (50).
6. Format averages to two decimal places, style the heading row and apply borders. Remove temporary calculations and save.
lessons.activity:
1. Enter at least five students with three numeric scores each.
2. Calculate Total and Average using cell references, not typed answers.
3. Copy formulas down with Fill Handle and inspect each row reference.
4. Format averages to two decimal places, add borders and format the header.

Sort: rearranges whole records. Filter: temporarily hides records that do not meet criteria.

lessons.introduction: Logical functions create consistent remarks from stated rules. The practice threshold of 75 is an exercise rule; confirm real grading policies with your teacher.
lessons.explanation:
IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false): chooses an output based on a condition.

AND returns TRUE only if every condition is TRUE. OR returns TRUE if at least one is TRUE.

Nested IF: an IF inside another IF; order descending thresholds carefully.

Text results require double quotes; >= includes the boundary value.

lessons.introduction: Consistent text and rounded results improve matching and readability. Keep original data beside cleaned data so changes can be audited.
lessons.explanation:
ROUND(number,digits) rounds to the nearest stated precision; ROUNDUP rounds away from zero and ROUNDDOWN towards zero.

LEN counts characters. LEFT/RIGHT extract from an end; MID(text,start,count) extracts from a position.

PROPER capitalizes words, UPPER uses uppercase, LOWER uses lowercase. Verify real names because automatic case conversion can be inappropriate.

TRIM removes extra ordinary spaces; pasted nonbreaking spaces may need separate cleaning. CONCAT joins values; legacy CONCATENATE and & also join; TEXTJOIN adds a delimiter where available.
lessons.guided_practice:
1. Enter inconsistent names in A2:A6, IDs such as ab-001 in B2:B6 and decimal grades in C2:C6. Keep these original columns.

5. Join ID and name with =E2&" - "&D2. Compare CONCAT/CONCATENATE and, where supported, =TEXTJOIN(" - ",TRUE,E2,D2). Use LOWER on a practice code to compare case.
6. Copy formulas down, compare original and cleaned records, label every transformation and save.

lessons.introduction: Lookup formulas retrieve a record using a stable key such as a student ID. Exact matching avoids returning a plausible but incorrect student.
lessons.explanation:
VLOOKUP(key,table,column,FALSE): finds an exact key in the first column and returns a value from a column to its right.

HLOOKUP searches the first row of a horizontal table and returns from a numbered row.

XLOOKUP searches one range and returns from a parallel range; exact match is the default. It is unavailable in Excel 2016 and 2019.

IFERROR(value,fallback): substitutes a readable message for an error; investigate the cause before masking it.

lessons.introduction: Fixed references keep shared assumptions stable while formulas are copied. Weighted results reflect component importance when weights total 100%.

lessons.introduction: PivotTables group many records into a summary without changing source rows. Choosing Average instead of Sum is essential for interpreting score data.
lessons.explanation:
PivotTable: an interactive grouped summary of a source dataset.

Rows and Columns define categories; Values hold an aggregation; Filters restrict the summary.

Refresh: recalculates the PivotTable from its current source. An Excel Table source expands with added records.

Grouping combines compatible categories or dates; mixed text/date entries can prevent date grouping.

lessons.introduction: Protecting a template reduces accidental changes; formula auditing helps locate genuine calculation problems. Sheet protection is not encryption or a privacy guarantee.
lessons.explanation:

Protect Workbook: protects workbook structure such as adding, removing or moving sheets; it differs from sheet protection and file encryption.

lessons.introduction: A recorded macro repeats a small task. This introductory lesson records only formatting in your own disposable workbook; uploaded VBA is never executed or automatically inspected by CodeLab.
lessons.explanation:
Macro: stored instructions that automate actions. VBA is the language used by Excel desktop macros.

Recorder: translates performed actions into recorded instructions; it can capture unintended steps too.

Absolute macro references target fixed cells; Use Relative References records movement relative to the starting cell.

.xlsx cannot retain VBA macros; .xlsm can. Excel for the web cannot create or run VBA macros.
lessons.guided_practice:
1. Use a school-authorized Excel desktop installation and your own blank practice workbook. Keep existing macro protections enabled; if recording/running is blocked, use the documented no-macro alternative below.
2. Create a small report with a title and table. Open View > Macros > Record Macro (or Developer > Record Macro), name it FormatReport and store it in This Workbook, not Personal Macro Workbook.
3. Record only formatting: bold the title, set a readable size and apply borders to the known table range. Stop Recording immediately after the intended changes.
4. Undo/revert formatting on a practice copy, then run only the macro you just recorded through View > Macros > View Macros > FormatReport > Run. Confirm only intended cells changed.
5. Discuss fixed versus Use Relative References recording; test relative movement only on a disposable copy. Do not download macros, trust unknown files or change global security settings.
6. Save as Excel Macro-Enabled Workbook (.xlsm) only when the macro is included. If policy blocks macros, perform the formatting manually, save .xlsx and explain the limitation and planned recorder steps in your reflection; never claim a macro ran.
